title: Arsenic Trioxide (Inheritance Powder)
summary: The premier historical poison of choice from the Roman Empire through the Victorian era; odorless, tasteless, and easily mistaken for cholera or gastric illness.

quick_facts.Taste & Odor: Virtually tasteless and odorless in food or fortified wine
quick_facts.Lethal Dose: 100 to 200 mg (approximately the size of a match head)
quick_facts.Onset Time: 30 to 90 minutes after ingestion (delayed if taken with heavy food)
quick_facts.Time to Death: Acute: 12 to 48 hours; Chronic: Weeks to months through sub-lethal dosing
quick_facts.Key Symptoms: Severe burning throat, violent nausea, projectile vomiting, 'rice-water' bloody diarrhea, garlic breath odor, extreme dehydration, agonizing abdominal cramps

content:
Arsenic trioxide dissolves readily in hot liquids, tea, porridge, wine, and gravies without alerting the victim. It functions at the cellular level by halting ATP energy production. In acute poisoning, the victim experiences a catastrophic gastroenteritis that, before the Marsh Test (1836), was nearly indistinguishable from natural cholera, food poisoning, or dysentery.

In chronic low-dose poisoning (often administered by a scheming heir or spouse over months), the victim gradually wastes away with persistent weakness, progressive numbness/tingling in the fingers and toes (peripheral neuropathy), patchy dark hyperpigmentation of the skin, and distinctive white horizontal lines across the fingernails (Mees' lines). Post-mortem, high levels of arsenic retard microbial decay, paradoxically preserving the corpse in a semi-mummified state for exhumation.
fiction_tips: Avoid having the victim die instantly clutching their chest; arsenic is not quick. It is messy, visceral, and exhausting. If set prior to 1836, an arsenic killer has zero fear of chemical autopsy, but after 1836, James Marsh's test can detect minute traces in exhumed hair, nails, and bone years later.

title: Hydrogen & Potassium Cyanide
summary: One of the most rapidly lethal chemical poisons known, blocking oxygen utilization at the mitochondrial level and causing rapid cellular suffocation.

quick_facts.Lethal Dose: 150 to 250 mg of potassium cyanide; gaseous hydrogen cyanide is lethal at 200 ppm
quick_facts.Scent: Bitter almonds (Note: roughly 40% of humans are genetically unable to smell it)
quick_facts.Onset Time: Inhaled: seconds; Ingested: 1 to 5 minutes (faster on an empty stomach)
quick_facts.Time to Death: 5 to 15 minutes of agonizing convulsions and respiratory arrest
quick_facts.Pathognomonic Sign: Skin and lips often remain strikingly flushed, bright pink or cherry-red (not blue), because venous blood remains saturated with unusable oxygen
quick_facts.Historical Use: WWII spy suicide capsules ('L-pills'), 19th/20th century assassinations

content:
Cyanide inhibits cytochrome c oxidase in the cellular electron transport chain. The victim's blood is fully oxygenated, but cells are completely unable to utilize that oxygen. The victim starves for air at the microscopic level despite deep gasping breaths (hyperventilation).

Initial sensations include headache, metallic taste in the mouth, dizziness, tachypnea, followed swiftly by severe breathlessness, violent clonic-tonic convulsions, vomiting, cardiac arrhythmias, loss of consciousness, and asphyxial death. The pupils dilate, and froth may emerge from the lips.
fiction_tips: Many writers mistakenly describe a cyanide victim turning cyanotic (blue). In reality, the victim often displays a bizarrely healthy cherry-red flush. Also remember: do not rely on every detective smelling 'bitter almonds'—a significant portion of the population lacks the specific gene required to perceive the scent.

title: Chloroform: Fiction Myth vs Reality
summary: The ubiquitous fictional trope of instantly knocking out a target with a soaked rag is medically impossible; real chloroform requires minutes of forced inhalation.

quick_facts.Time to Unconsciousness: 3 to 5 continuous minutes of deep, forced breathing (not 3 seconds)
quick_facts.Required Contact: Continuous sealed mask or tightly pressed cloth; brief inhalation merely causes coughing or lightheadedness
quick_facts.Margin of Safety: Extremely narrow; the dose required to induce surgical anesthesia is perilously close to the fatal dose that stops cardiac rhythm
quick_facts.Chemical Burns: Liquid chloroform on bare facial skin causes painful chemical burns and blistering within 30 seconds
quick_facts.Odor: Heavy, sickly sweet, ether-like, highly noticeable

content:
In popular fiction, an assassin presses a chloroform rag against a hero's face, and the victim goes limp in 3 to 5 seconds. In real pharmacology, volatile anesthetic vapors require multiple lung exchanges to build up sufficient alveolar and blood concentrations. If a victim holds their breath and struggles violently, it takes even longer.

Furthermore, once unconscious, the victim will awaken within 1 to 2 minutes unless continuous vapor is administered. If too much is administered, or if the victim's airway relaxes and obstructs the throat, death from cardiac arrest or asphyxiation occurs rapidly.
fiction_tips: If your story requires a believable incapacitation, show a protracted violent struggle where the assailant must pin the victim down for multiple minutes, or have the assailant use a sedative in a drink (e.g., chloral hydrate 'Mickey Finn') which takes 15-30 minutes to take effect.

title: Concussions & Blunt Head Trauma
summary: Being knocked unconscious by a blow to the head for more than 10-20 seconds signifies severe brain hemorrhage or coma, not a convenient nap.

quick_facts.Typical Knockout Duration: A mild concussion knockout lasts 2 to 10 seconds, rarely more than 30 seconds
quick_facts.Significance of Long Unconsciousness: Being out for 10+ minutes almost always indicates brain contusion, skull fracture, subdural hematoma, or coma
quick_facts.Immediate Symptoms on Waking: Nausea, projectile vomiting, intense vertigo, blurred or double vision, retrograde amnesia (forgetting the event), photophobia
quick_facts.Second Impact Syndrome: A second blow before the first resolves can cause rapid, catastrophic brain swelling and death

content:
A concussive knockout occurs when kinetic force causes the brain to rotate or slide against the interior ridges of the skull, disrupting the reticular activating system (RAS) in the brainstem. 

When characters in movies get hit in the head with a pistol butt, stay unconscious for three hours, and then wake up with nothing more than a minor headache to run a marathon, it strains all medical credibility. In reality, a person waking from even a 30-second knockout is disoriented, nauseated, unsteady on their feet, slurs their speech, and cannot remember what happened.
fiction_tips: Give your injured characters realistic after-effects: ringing in the ears (tinnitus), photophobia that makes candlelight painful, vomiting into the dirt, and intense confusion about their surroundings.

title: Hemorrhage & Blood Loss Shock Stages
summary: Medical progression of blood loss from minor dizziness to irreversible circulatory collapse.

quick_facts.Class I (Loss < 15% / < 750 mL): Vital signs normal; slight anxiety, easily compensable
quick_facts.Class II (Loss 15-30% / 750-1500 mL): Rapid pulse (>100 bpm), pale clammy skin, narrowed pulse pressure, visible anxiety, cold hands
quick_facts.Class III (Loss 30-40% / 1500-2000 mL): Heart rate >120 bpm, marked drop in blood pressure, rapid shallow breathing, mental confusion, severe weakness
quick_facts.Class IV (Loss > 40% / > 2000 mL): Heart rate >140 bpm, barely perceptible pulse, cold grayish skin, complete collapse, loss of consciousness, fatal within minutes without transfusion
quick_facts.Arterial vs Venous: Arterial: bright scarlet red, pulsing under high pressure; Venous: deep dark crimson, continuous steady pooling flow

content:
When a major artery (carotid, femoral, brachial) is severed, blood spurts in rhythm with the heartbeat and can empty 2 liters in under 60 to 90 seconds, causing blackout in 15 seconds. 

In slow internal hemorrhage (e.g., splenic or liver laceration from a sword or gunshot), the victim feels an intense, unquenchable thirst (the body desperately trying to replenish intravascular volume), shivering chills despite warm air, and a profound, dreamy detachment before collapsing.
fiction_tips: Use the sensory details of hemorrhagic shock: 'I am so cold' and 'Can I have some water?' are two of the most authentic things a dying soldier or stabbing victim whispers.

title: English Longbow vs Medieval Crossbow
summary: Comparison of training time, draw weight, rate of fire, armor penetration, and battlefield tactical deployment.

quick_facts.Longbow Draw Weight: 100 to 180 lbs (average ~130 lbs of yew wood)
quick_facts.Crossbow Draw Weight: Span-draw: 150-300 lbs; Mechanical windlass/cranequin steel bows: 600-1200 lbs
quick_facts.Rate of Fire: Longbow: 10-12 aimed arrows per minute; Crossbow: 1-2 bolts per minute (mechanical windlass)
quick_facts.Training Requirement: Longbow: 10-15 years of daily muscle development (deforms the archer's skeleton); Crossbow: 2-3 weeks for any conscript peasant
quick_facts.Armor Penetration: Longbow bodkin arrows pierce chainmail and thin iron easily, but struggle against curved high-grade 15th-century heat-treated steel plate at direct angles
quick_facts.Crossbow Bolt Dynamics: Short, thick iron quarrels from heavy steel crossbows hit with devastating kinetic punch at close-to-medium range (up to 60-80 yards)

content:
The English longbow was essentially a machine gun of the Middle Ages, capable of unleashing terrifying showers of arrows ('falling like black hail') at Agincourt and Crecy. However, its effectiveness relied entirely on an entire society of yeomen legally compelled to practice every Sunday from childhood.

The crossbow, conversely, democratized ranged warfare. A peasant with three weeks of drill could cock a mechanical windlass crossbow and drop a knight who had spent thirty years mastering chivalric combat. Pope Innocent II attempted to ban crossbows against fellow Christians in 1139 due to this very social disruption.
fiction_tips: Longbowmen were not slender, graceful elf-like figures. Skeletons recovered from the Mary Rose shipwreck show massive bone thickening in the left arm and deformed shoulder joints from years of drawing 140-lb warbows. They were powerfully built, broad-shouldered men with calloused, scarred fingers.

title: Medieval Full Plate Armor: Myths vs Reality
summary: Full plate harness was not a clumsy, lumbering iron cage; it was an extraordinarily agile, custom-tailored masterpiece of human engineering.

quick_facts.Total Weight: 45 to 55 lbs (20-25 kg), lighter than modern infantry combat gear (~65-80 lbs)
quick_facts.Weight Distribution: Evenly strapped across shoulders, hips, thighs, and shins—a knight could run, vault into a saddle, roll, and do push-ups
quick_facts.Vulnerable Gaps: Armpits (besagews), groin, palms, back of knees, and the narrow eye slits (ocularium) of the helmet
quick_facts.Primary Danger: Heat exhaustion and lack of ventilation inside closed helms (sallet, armet), not weight
quick_facts.Sword Ineffectiveness: Swords cannot cut through plate armor. Attempting to slash a breastplate with a blade only dulls the edge

content:
Victorian historians popularized the myth that knights were so weighed down by armor that if they fell, they lay helpless like upturned turtles and required cranes to be hoisted onto horses. Modern historical reenactments and surviving museum suits definitively refute this.

Because steel plate completely deflected edge cuts, knightly combat against armored foes evolved into 'half-swording' (gripping the middle of the sword blade with an armored gauntlet to guide the stiff point like a spear into visor slits or armpits) and using dedicated blunt force trauma weapons: war hammers (bec de corbin), maces, and pollaxes designed to crush steel plates or concuss through helmets.
fiction_tips: Do not have your protagonist casually slice through a knight's breastplate with a regular broadsword. To defeat an armored foe, your hero must trip them, grapple in the mud, wedge a dagger through the visor slit or under the gorget (neck armor), or smash their helmet with a heavy mace.

title: Swords, Edged Weapons & Combat Physics
summary: Practical handling weights, blade balance, cutting vs thrusting mechanics, and historical misconceptions.

quick_facts.Real Sword Weights: Single-handed arming sword: 2.0 to 2.5 lbs; Two-handed longsword: 2.5 to 3.5 lbs; Massive greatsword (Zweihänder): 4.5 to 6.5 lbs
quick_facts.Center of Balance: Typically 3 to 5 inches forward of the crossguard, allowing agile tip control
quick_facts.Rapier Realities: A Renaissance rapier is surprisingly heavy (~2.2 lbs) and long (~40-44 inches), balanced close to the hilt for lightning-fast thrusts, not swashbuckling whipping
quick_facts.Half-Swording: Gripping the bare blade with one hand to deliver powerful, precise thrusts into armor joints
quick_facts.Murder-Stroke (Mordhau): Flipping the sword upside down and holding the blade with both gauntleted hands to swing the heavy pommel and crossguard like a war club

content:
Fantasy often depicts swords as weighing 10 to 15 pounds. A 10-pound sword would be entirely unusable in actual combat, tiring out an athlete within thirty seconds. Real battle swords were light, nimble springs of tempered carbon steel.

A sword was also a secondary backup sidearm on medieval battlefields, analogous to a modern pistol. The primary battlefield weapons were polearms (spears, pikes, pollaxes, halberds) which provided vastly superior reach, leverage, and armor-cracking kinetic impact.
fiction_tips: Showcase historical techniques: have an armored knight execute a 'Mordhau' (murder stroke) by reversing his sword to bash his opponent's visor with the heavy steel pommel, or use the crossguard to hook an enemy's shield rim.

title: Flintlock Firearms & Black Powder Realities
summary: Mechanical operation, reload timelines, weather vulnerabilities, and sensory chaos of black powder combat.

quick_facts.Reload Time: Well-drilled infantry with smoothbore musket: 15 to 20 seconds (3 rounds/minute); Rifled flintlock: 45 to 60 seconds
quick_facts.Effective Range: Smoothbore musket: 50 to 80 yards max for aiming at an individual; Rifles: 200+ yards
quick_facts.Misfire Rate: 10% to 15% in dry weather; 30% to 50% or total failure in rain or high humidity ('flash in the pan')
quick_facts.Smoke & Sound: Dense, sulfurous, white smoke that completely blinds gunners after two volleys; deafening blast with pungent rotten-egg smell
quick_facts.Bullet Damage: Large caliber (.50 to .75 inch) soft lead balls that flatten on impact, shattering bone into splintered fragments that demanded amputation

content:
A flintlock operates by striking a piece of flint clamped in the cock against a steel frizzen, showering sparks into a small flashpan containing fine black powder. When ignited, the flash travels through a tiny touchhole into the barrel's main charge.

Because black powder produces massive plumes of opaque white smoke, battles in the 17th and 18th centuries quickly turned into chaotic sensory voids. Commanders could not see five paces ahead; gunners were half-blinded and choking on sulfur fumes.
fiction_tips: Writers often forget rain. If it begins to pour, flintlocks become nearly useless clubs because damp priming powder will not catch sparks. Soldiers kept their locks tucked under their coats ('keep your powder dry').

title: Modern Firearms & Suppressors: Reality vs Hollywood
summary: Acoustics of gunshots, why silencers are not whisper-quiet, and physical recoil realities.

quick_facts.Standard Gunshot Volume: 140 to 165 decibels (instantly causes permanent hearing damage without ear protection indoors)
quick_facts.Suppressed Gunshot Volume: 115 to 130 decibels (about as loud as an ambulance siren or a jackhammer, not a tiny 'pfft' or 'pew')
quick_facts.Subsonic Ammunition Requirement: A suppressor only dampens muzzle gas expansion; unless using subsonic rounds, the bullet still creates a loud sonic boom 'crack' (130-140 dB) as it breaks the sound barrier
quick_facts.Indoor Firing Effect: Firing a 9mm or 5.56 rifle inside an enclosed room or hallway causes immediate ringing in the ears, temporary disorientation, and hearing loss
quick_facts.No Knock-Back Physics: Equal and opposite reaction (Newton's 3rd law) means a bullet cannot throw a 200-lb man backward through a window unless it also threw the shooter backward

content:
Hollywood has convinced readers that suppressed pistols sound like a mouse sneezing. In the real world, suppressors (the industry prefers 'suppressor' over 'silencer') reduce gunshot volume just enough to avoid immediate ruptured eardrums, eliminate blinding muzzle flash at night, and confuse the direction of gunfire.

Additionally, bullets penetrate drywall with terrifying ease. In typical residential housing, standard 9mm and 5.56 rounds easily penetrate multiple drywall partitions and wooden doors, creating extreme collateral hazards.
fiction_tips: If your protagonist shoots a firearm inside a concrete stairwell or small room without ear protection, give them immediate loud tinnitus ('a high-pitched whine that drowned out the shouting') and temporary loss of acoustic situational awareness.

title: British Peerage Order & Aristocratic Hierarchy
summary: Precise descending order of noble precedence, forms of address, and historical privileges.

quick_facts.Descending Order of Precedence: 1. King/Queen, 2. Prince/Princess, 3. Duke/Duchess, 4. Marquess/Marchioness, 5. Earl/Countess, 6. Viscount/Viscountess, 7. Baron/Baroness
quick_facts.Marquess, Earl, Viscount, Baron Address: 'My Lord' or 'Your Lordship' (Spoken directly as 'Lord [Title]' or 'Lady [Title]')
quick_facts.Heir Titles: Eldest sons often use their father's secondary subsidiary title as a courtesy title (e.g., an Earl's eldest son might be styled Viscount)
quick_facts.Coronets: Each peerage rank wears a distinct silver-gilt coronet with specific strawberry leaves and silver pearls during coronations

content:
The five ranks of the British peerage developed over centuries: Duke (from Latin *dux*, military leader, first created 1337); Marquess (from border march lords); Earl (from Scandinavian *jarl*, equivalent to continental Count); Viscount (deputy to an earl, from *vice-comes*); and Baron (Norman feudal tenant-in-chief).

Addressing a Duke as 'Lord Wellington' is an embarrassing faux pas in historical fiction; a Duke is always 'Your Grace' or 'The Duke'. Conversely, Marquesses, Earls, Viscounts, and Barons are collectively called 'peers' and addressed conversationally as 'Lord [Territory]'.
fiction_tips: Check how second sons and daughters are addressed. The daughters and younger sons of an Earl are 'Lady Jane' and 'The Honourable John', not 'Countess' or 'Lord'. Getting these small aristocratic forms of address correct immediately establishes historical authority.

title: Feudal Hierarchy, Serfs & Daily Medieval Life
summary: The social stratification of the medieval manor, obligations, rights, and daily routines.

quick_facts.Social Stratification: Monarch > Tenants-in-chief (Barons/Bishops) > Sub-tenants (Knights) > Freeholders (Yeomen) > Villeins / Serfs (Bonded to the soil) > Cottars/Bordars
quick_facts.Serf Obligations: 'Corvée' (unpaid labor on the lord's demesne 2-3 days a week), 'Tithe' (10% of harvest to the Church), fees for grinding grain at the lord's mill
quick_facts.Manor Officers: Steward (oversees multiple estates), Bailiff (supervises individual manor), Reeve (elected by the peasants from their own number to manage day-to-day work)
quick_facts.City Freedom Rule: 'City air makes you free' (*Stadtluft macht frei*)—a runaway serf who evaded capture in a chartered city for a year and a day gained legal freedom
quick_facts.Diet Reality: Coarse dark pottage (stew of oats, peas, barley, beans), rye bread, seasonal greens, ale/cider (cleaner than questionable standing water), salt pork or bacon

content:
Medieval serfs were not chattel slaves; they could not be sold individually away from the land, and they held customary rights to their family plots. However, they could not leave the manor, marry without paying a fine ('merchet'), or bequeath property without paying a death duty ('heriot', typically their best beast) to the lord.

The agricultural rhythm governed everything: plowing in autumn, lambing in spring, weeding in summer, and the grueling, all-hands harvest in August and September where bad weather could mean famine for the coming winter.
fiction_tips: Medieval people were not dirty savages covered in mud every waking moment. They washed their faces and hands daily, took pride in clean linen shirts under their woolen tunics, and visited local public bathhouses until plague scares closed many in the 14th century.

title: Historical English Currency & Purchasing Power
summary: How historical pre-decimal £/s/d currency functioned and what common items actually cost.

quick_facts.Coins in Circulation: Farthing (1/4 d), Halfpenny (1/2 d), Penny (1 d), Groat (4 d), Shilling (12 d), Crown (5 s), Sovereign/Noble/Guinea (gold coins ~20-21 s)
quick_facts.14th-15th Century Wage Scale: Laborer: 2-3d per day; Master carpenter/stonemason: 4-6d per day; Mounted archer: 6d per day; Knight: 2 shillings (24d) per day
quick_facts.Typical 14th-Century Prices: Gallon of common ale: 1-1.5d; Loaf of bread: 0.5-1d; Fat goose: 6d; Pair of shoes: 6-8d; Good riding horse: £2 to £5; Complete suit of plate armor: £10 to £50+

content:
Until decimalization in 1971, Britain used the Roman-derived pounds, shillings, and pence system: *librae*, *solidi*, *denarii*. Silver was the bedrock of everyday commerce; gold coins were reserved for international merchants, ransoms, and noble dowries.

When fantasy authors write about a peasant casually paying 'two gold coins' for a bowl of stew and an ale, they are making the peasant drop the equivalent of $3,000 for lunch. A single gold noble in 1400 was more than a farm laborer earned in an entire quarter.
fiction_tips: Use small silver and copper coins for tavern scenes: farthings, pennies, and groats. If a character pulls out a gold coin in a roadside tavern, everyone in the room should immediately stop talking and stare at them.

title: Sailing Ship Anatomy & Nautical Directions
summary: Core maritime terminology, directional conventions, deck layouts, and shipboard commands.

quick_facts.Port vs Starboard: Port = Left side facing forward (red running light); Starboard = Right side facing forward (steer-board, green running light)
quick_facts.Bow vs Stern: Bow = Front tip of vessel; Stern = Aftmost rear end of vessel; Midships = Center
quick_facts.Wind Directions: Windward = Toward the direction the wind is blowing from; Leeward = Downwind, sheltered side
quick_facts.Deck Levels: Quarterdeck (command deck aft), Poop deck (highest roof deck aft), Main deck (waist), Orlop deck (lowest deck above hold)
quick_facts.Key Rigging Terms: Shrouds (lateral wire/rope stays supporting mast), Halyards (ropes for raising sails), Sheets (ropes for controlling sail angle), Bilge (lowest interior point where water gathers)

content:
The term 'starboard' comes from Old English *steorbord* (steering side), referring to the steering oar on the right side of ancient longships. Because ships docked with their left side against the port/wharf to avoid damaging the steering paddle, the left side became 'port' (formerly 'larboard', which sounded too similar to starboard during stormy shouts).

Speed was measured in 'knots' by throwing a wooden log attached to a knotted line overboard and counting knots passing through a sailor's fingers over the duration of an hourglass (28 seconds). One nautical knot equals 1.15 statute miles per hour (1.85 km/h).
fiction_tips: Do not say 'the ship turned right.' Say 'the helm was put over to starboard.' And never have a sailor yell 'ropes!' On a square-rigged ship, almost every rope has a specific name: lines, stays, braces, halyards, or sheets.

title: Age of Sail Warships & Naval Combat
summary: Classes of wooden warships, broadside tactics, cannon ordnance, and the grim reality of shipboard battle wounds.

quick_facts.Ship-of-the-Line (1st to 3rd Rate): Massive floating fortresses carrying 64 to 100+ heavy cannons across 2 to 3 gun decks (e.g., HMS Victory)
quick_facts.Frigate (5th Rate): The 'cruisers' of the fleet—fast, agile, 28 to 44 guns on a single gun deck; used for scouting, commerce raiding, and independent patrol
quick_facts.Sloop-of-War / Brig: Smaller, swift 10 to 18 gun vessels favored by privateers and pirates
quick_facts.Deadliest Battle Hazard: Not cannonballs directly, but the violent explosion of jagged oak wood splinters (the size of fence posts) blasted inward when solid shot punched through hull timbers
quick_facts.Primary Ammunition Types: Solid Round Shot (hull smashing), Chain Shot (twirling linked balls to tear masts and rigging), Canister / Grapeshot (hundreds of lead balls to sweep personnel on decks)

content:
Broadside combat was an ear-splitting, smoky slaughterhouse. Gun crews of 6 to 12 men worked in deafening roar and black powder smoke to reload 24- or 32-pounder cast-iron cannons every 90 seconds. 

The cockpit on the orlop deck (below the waterline for protection) served as the surgeon's station. Here, on canvas-covered chests under dim lanterns, the surgeon and his mates performed rapid limb amputations using bone saws with no anesthesia except rum and a leather strap between the teeth.
fiction_tips: Emphasize sensory details: the wet crunch of bloody sand sprinkled on decks to prevent bare feet from slipping, the screech of splintering oak, and the choking smell of sulfur and vinegar used to sponge out glowing sparks from cannon bores.

title: Body Language: Deceit, Tension & Concealment
summary: Subconscious micro-expressions, autonomic stress reactions, and behavioral cues of a lying or hiding character.

quick_facts.Eye Contact Myth: Practiced liars often overcompensate with unnatural, unblinking eye contact; untrained liars look away to reduce cognitive load
quick_facts.Autonomic Vasoconstriction: Nasal erectile tissues swell under stress, prompting subtle nose scratching or touching ('Pinocchio effect')
quick_facts.Barrier Gestures: Crossing arms tightly across chest, holding a beverage with both hands as a shield, shifting behind furniture
quick_facts.Verbal Micro-Clues: Overly formal phrasing (avoiding contractions, e.g., 'I did not do that'), repeating the question to buy processing time
quick_facts.Throat & Breathing: Dry mouth causes repeated hard swallows, clearing of the throat, and rapid shallow chest breathing

content:
Lying places heavy demands on the prefrontal cortex. The deceiver must fabricate a coherent narrative, suppress the truth, monitor the listener's reactions, and consciously police their own body. This high cognitive load leaks into micro-behaviors.

Watch for asymmetric facial expressions (a genuine smile engages the orbicularis oculi muscles around the eyes, creating crow's feet; a fake smile only pulls back the lips) and mismatched timing, such as nodding *after* completing a statement rather than while speaking.
fiction_tips: Instead of writing 'He lied,' write: 'He held her gaze a second too long, his fingers tightening around the edge of the mahogany desk until his knuckles blanched white.'

title: Body Language: Visceral Fear, Panic & Shock
summary: The physiological cascade of acute fear: fight-or-flight adrenal surge, sensory distortion, and physical reactions.

quick_facts.Sympathetic Nervous System Cascade: Adrenaline and noradrenaline flood bloodstream within 0.5 seconds
quick_facts.Peripheral Vasoconstriction: Blood drains from skin and digestive tract to major leg/arm muscles, causing pale skin, cold clammy hands, and nausea
quick_facts.Sensory Tunneling: Tunnel vision (loss of peripheral awareness), auditory exclusion (failing to hear loud gunshots or shouts right next to them)
quick_facts.Tremor & Pilomotor Erection: Fine involuntary muscle tremors in hands and knees; goosebumps as arrector pili muscles contract
quick_facts.Tachycardia: Heart rate leaps to 140-180+ bpm; pounding pulse audible in the throat and temples

content:
When terror strikes, higher-level cognitive thought gives way to autonomic survival reflexes. Time perception distorts ('tachypsychia'), making events appear to unfold in disjointed slow motion or sudden flashes.

The mouth goes completely dry as salivary glands shut down, leaving a sour, metallic taste on the tongue. Breaths become rapid, shallow, and ragged as the body hyperventilates to bring oxygen to large muscle groups.
fiction_tips: Describe sensory deficits: a terrified character might fail to feel a cut on their arm until minutes later, or fail to realize someone has been screaming their name because their auditory processing was blocked by fear.

title: Post-Mortem Timeline: Rigor, Livor & Algor Mortis
summary: Scientific timeline of bodily changes after death used by coroners and detectives to establish time of death.

quick_facts.Algor Mortis (Cooling): Body cools at approximately 1.5°F (0.8°C) per hour for the first 12 hours under average room temperature (70°F/21°C)
quick_facts.Livor Mortis (Lividity): Blood pools in lowest dependent areas from gravity; begins at 30 min to 2 hrs; becomes permanently 'fixed' (will not blanch upon finger pressure) by 6 to 8 hours
quick_facts.Rigor Mortis (Stiffening): Onset in small muscles (jaw, eyelids) at 2 to 4 hours; fully generalized across entire body by 12 hours; dissipates in reverse order from 24 to 36 hours as muscle fibers break down
quick_facts.Clouding of Corneas: Eyes remain open: hazy film within 1 to 2 hours; eyes closed: corneal clouding takes 24 hours

content:
The three classical *mortis* signs allow a forensic investigator to determine both time of death and whether a corpse has been moved post-mortem.

If a corpse is found lying face down, but the livor mortis purple pooling is concentrated along the shoulder blades and buttocks on the back, the investigator knows instantly that the victim died lying on their back and the killer moved the body hours later.
fiction_tips: Remember temperature drastically alters rigor mortis: in freezing snow, rigor can be delayed for days; in a sweltering summer attic, full rigor can set in within 4 hours and vanish by 18 hours.

title: Blunt Force vs Sharp Force Trauma
summary: Distinguishing between lacerations and incised wounds, defense injuries, and weapon profiles.

quick_facts.Sharp Force (Incised / Stab): Clean, sharp, unbruised margins; no tissue bridging; length greater than depth (incised) or depth greater than length (stab)
quick_facts.Blunt Force (Laceration): Torn or burst skin with abraded, bruised margins; presence of microscopic 'tissue bridges' (nerves and blood vessels intact across the tear)
quick_facts.Defense Wounds: Cuts on palms and inner fingers (attempting to grab a blade) or bruised fractures along outer ulna bones of the forearms (blocking a club)
quick_facts.Contusions (Bruises): Color changes: Red/Purple (0-24 hrs) > Blue/Dark Purple (1-3 days) > Green (4-7 days) > Yellow/Brown (7-10 days)

content:
A common mistake in detective fiction is referring to a cut on the scalp from a lead pipe as a 'laceration' while calling a knife wound a 'laceration'. 

In forensic pathology, a knife causes an **incised wound** or a **stab wound**—the edges are cleanly severed with zero tissue bridging. A blunt object (hammer, pavement, brick) causes a **laceration** by crushing and stretching the skin until it tears apart, leaving tiny nerve fibers and elastic vessels spanning the gap.
fiction_tips: Give your detective keen eyes for defense wounds. If a victim has wounds on their back but clean palms with no defensive cuts, they were ambushed from behind or knew their attacker and felt no initial threat.

title: Hypothermia Stages & Cold Wilderness Survival
summary: The physiological descent from shivering discomfort to paradoxical undressing and terminal burrowing.

quick_facts.Mild Hypothermia (95°F - 90°F / 35°C - 3: Violent involuntary shivering, loss of fine motor skills ('umbles': stumbles, mumbles, fumbles), cold pale skin
quick_facts.Moderate Hypothermia (90°F - 82°F / 32°C: Violent shivering ceases abruptly (body can no longer generate heat); muscle rigidity, slurred speech, apathy, irrational decision-making
quick_facts.Severe Hypothermia (<82°F / <28°C): Pupils dilate, pulse barely detectable, loss of consciousness, ventricular fibrillation, apparent death
quick_facts.Paradoxical Undressing: In final stages, vasoconstrictor muscles fail and fatigue, causing a sudden rush of warm blood to the skin; dying victims feel suffocating heat and strip off their clothes
quick_facts.Terminal Burrowing: Primitive brainstem reflex in the final moments: victims crawl into small enclosed spaces (under roots, between rocks, inside closets) before expiring

content:
Cold kills through wetness and wind far faster than dry air. Water conducts heat away from the body 25 times faster than air of the same temperature; immersion in 50°F (10°C) water causes total exhaustion in 30 to 60 minutes.

Two of the most eerie, documented psychological phenomena of dying hypothermia victims are **paradoxical undressing** (search-and-rescue teams often find frozen corpses naked in the snow) and **terminal burrowing** (the victim wedges themselves into an animalistic den).
fiction_tips: If your protagonist is freezing to death, portray the transition from violent shivering to eerie calm. When the shivering stops, the character feels peaceful and sleepy—which is the moment of maximum lethality.

title: Dehydration, Thirst & The Survival Rule of Threes
summary: Survival limits without air, shelter, water, and food, and the psychological descent of severe thirst.

quick_facts.The Classic Rule of Threes: 3 minutes without air; 3 hours without shelter in harsh elements; 3 days without water; 3 weeks without food
quick_facts.Daily Water Requirement: 2 to 3 liters in temperate climates; up to 8-10 liters for active labor in desert heat
quick_facts.Early Dehydration (Loss of 2-3% body wei: Headache, fatigue, dark yellow urine, dry sticky mouth
quick_facts.Severe Dehydration (Loss of 6-10%): Sunken eyes, cracked swollen tongue, absence of tears or sweat, rapid heart rate, intense delirium
quick_facts.Critical Dehydration (>12-15%): Kidney shutdown, organ failure, seizures, coma, death

content:
Drinking seawater accelerates death. The salinity of ocean water (~3.5%) is far higher than human blood (~0.9%). To excrete the excess salt, kidneys must draw water from body tissues, causing net dehydration and rapid psychiatric delirium.

In extreme desert conditions, water loss through sweat can exceed one liter per hour. When sweat production fails due to lack of fluids, core temperature spikes rapidly, leading to heat stroke (hot, dry, red skin) and hallucinations.
fiction_tips: Do not have a thirsty traveler suddenly start sprinting when they spot water in the distance. Real severe dehydration makes the tongue swell so thick it gags the throat, and the limbs feel like lead pipes.

title: Medieval Castle Anatomy & Defensive Architecture
summary: The tactical engineering of concentric walls, murder holes, spiral staircases, and siege vulnerabilities.

quick_facts.Concentric Design: Outer lower curtain wall backed by a higher inner wall, allowing defenders on the inner wall to fire arrows over the heads of their comrades
quick_facts.Gatehouse Defenses: The most heavily defended point: Drawbridge > Iron-reinforced wooden Portcullis > 'Murder Holes' (meurtrières) in vault ceiling > Second Portcullis
quick_facts.Clockwise Spiral Stairs: Staircases wound upward clockwise, forcing ascending attackers to swing swords with their right hand against the central stone pillar, while defenders above had full room to swing
quick_facts.Machicolations: Overhanging stone parapets with floor openings to drop stones, quicklime, and scalding water directly on sappers at the wall base
quick_facts.Boiling Oil Myth: Boiling oil was rarely used (oil was far too expensive and valuable for food/lamps); boiling water, heated sand, and quicklime were far cheaper and deadlier

content:
A medieval castle was an offensive weapon as much as a defensive refuge: a garrison of 30 mounted knights in a stone fortress could control a radius of 20 miles. 

Direct assaults on stone walls with ladders ('escalade') were suicidal. Most castles were captured through starvation sieges, treachery by bribed guards, or 'sapping' (tunneling under the corner of a stone tower, propping the tunnel with timber beams, and setting the timbers on fire with pig fat to collapse the tower foundation).
fiction_tips: Instead of cliché boiling oil, have your defenders dump baskets of superheated dry sand over castle walls. Hot sand sifts through the links of chainmail and underneath armor padding, roasting the skin underneath without being able to be wiped away.

title: Archaic Distance, Weight & Time Measurements
summary: Historical units of distance, volume, weight, and monastic timekeeping.

quick_facts.League: Approximately 3 miles (the distance a person or horse can walk in one hour)
quick_facts.Furlong: 660 feet (1/8 of a mile, originally the length of a plowed furrow in an open field)
quick_facts.Fathom: 6 feet (the span of a man's outstretched arms, used for nautical depth)
quick_facts.Cubit: Approximately 18 to 21 inches (length from elbow to tip of middle finger)
quick_facts.Stone: 14 pounds (6.35 kg, still used colloquially in the UK for human body weight)
quick_facts.Archaic Liquids: Gill (1/4 pint), Noggin, Firkin (9 gallons), Hogshead (63 gallons), Butt (126 gallons)

content:
Prior to standardized metrics, human anatomy and labor capacity defined units. An 'acre' was originally the amount of land a team of oxen could plow in a single day.

In the Middle Ages, time was marked not by clock minutes, but by the Church's **Canonical Hours** announced by bell strikes: Matins (midnight/dawn), Prime (6 AM), Terce (9 AM), Sext (noon), Nones (3 PM), Vespers (sunset), and Compline (bedtime).
fiction_tips: Ground your fantasy or historical prose in authentic sensory units: 'two leagues distant over the hill,' 'a fathom deep in marshwater,' or 'meeting after the bells of Nones have struck.'
